insertions.anchor_context:
Galifard, the steward. These servants being elderly persons, the
Baroness, who was possessed of a pleasant humor, had christened them
Mother Sabine and Father Galifard.

The features of Mother Sabine bore the imprint of her amiable
disposition; she was as open and candid as Father Galifard was sly and
dissimulating. The plausible air of the steward might deceive persons
without much experience; but close observers could easily discover the
most perverse inclinations under his false mask of good nature. There
was duplicity in his great blue eyes, anger concentrated in his nostrils,
something wily in the end of his tapering nose, and malice in the shape
of his lips.

CHAPTER III.

IN WHICH ARE SHOWN THE GOODNESS OF MOTHER
SABINE AND THE WICKEDNESS OF FATHER
GALIFARD.


Mother Sabine, worthy of the confidence which had been reposed in her,
displayed for Mistifou a truly maternal tenderness; she tended him,
coddled him, took such pains with him, in short, that he became one of
the most beautiful cats in that quarter of the town where the cats are
magnificent. She watched over him constantly, gave him the choicest bits
to eat, and put him to bed at night on the softest of eider-down quilts.
insertions.fact: Mother Sabine is established as amiable and good; later the heading names cruelty instead.

He was a living proof of the influence of
good fare upon the race. He owed his excellent condition chiefly to
Mother Sabine, whom he held in affectionate consideration; he showed, on
the other hand, for Father Galifard a very marked dislike. As if he had
divined that here he had to do with an enemy, he refused to accept
anything presented by the steward. However, they saw but little of each
other. The days passed very happily with Mistifou, and everything
promised a smiling future for him; but, like the sword of Damocles,
troubles are ever suspended above the heads of men and of cats.
insertions.violation_context:
The cat was not the evil one--Providence had protected him.


CHAPTER V.

IN WHICH THE CAT CONTENDS
SUCCESSFULLY AGAINST
HIS ENEMY.


The events we have recorded indicate very clearly the position of our
personages. Fearing to lose both the well-beloved cat and the advantages
she was ambitious to obtain, Mother Sabine redoubled her vigilance and
attention.

CHAPTER VI.

HOW FATHER GALIFARD CONFIDES HIS ODIOUS PLANS
TO NICHOLAS FANFRELUCHE.


Father Galifard searched for an accomplice. He at first thought of
finding one among the domestics of the household; but he reflected that
they all were devoted to Mother Sabine, and were capable of betraying
him, and causing him to be shamefully turned out of the mansion, in which
he held so honorable and lucrative a post. However, he had great desire
for an accomplice.

He was

insertions.violation_quote_edited:
He was
very anxious to warn his judge, and sought an excuse to steal off.
insertions.violation_context:
As soon as Madame de la Rochefleur learned how Mistifou had been
recovered, she ordered young Fanfreluche to be brought before her.

"I'll go and look him up," said Father Galifard, with alacrity. He was
very anxious to warn his accomplice, and sought an excuse to steal off.

"No, remain! You have admitted him to the mansion, you shall see him
turned away, and will learn to bestow your confidence more wisely in
future."

insertions.anchor_context:
Mistifou, knowing henceforth with whom he had to deal, promised himself
to avoid the steward, or to fight him, if need be, with tooth and nail.

As to Father Galifard, it was enough that his projects had been defeated,
in order that he should persist in them with desperation. He now wished
the destruction of the poor and innocent cat, not only on account of his
jealousy of Mother Sabine, but because he hated the cat itself.

"Oh, what humiliation!" he said to himself, with bitterness.

CHAPTER VII.

IN WHICH FATHER GALIFARD IS ON THE POINT OF
ACCOMPLISHING HIS PURPOSE, AND MOTHER SABINE'S
CAT IS IN AN UNPLEASANT PREDICAMENT.


Galifard had fixed the following day for the cruel execution of Mistifou,
for he knew that Mother Sabine on that day was to carry to the express
office a package destined for her sister.

All the forenoon and afternoon Fanfreluche was plunged in the darkest
despondency, and when the fatal hour sounded, he was assailed by the
irresolutions of the previous day. When Mother Sabine, before going out,
said to him, "I leave Mistifou in your charge; you must take care of him,
and make him play, so that he will not fret too much during my absence,"
the poor lad felt his heart fail, and his natural loyalty revolted.
insertions.fact: Galifard plans Mistifou's destruction; later the planned execution becomes a coronation.
